lifeText.text: Bashō was born Matsuo Kinsaku near Ueno in [Iga Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iga_Province), into a family of samurai descent and modest means. In his late teens he went into service with Tōdō Yoshitada, a young lord who shared his taste for haikai, and wrote under the name Sōbō. Yoshitada’s sudden death in 1666 ended that life. What Bashō did next is mostly guesswork, though his poems kept turning up in anthologies.

Around 1672 he moved to Edo, and within a few years he was a professional haikai master with twenty disciples. In the winter of 1680 he did something odd for a success: he moved across the river to Fukagawa, where his students built him a hut and planted a banana tree, a *bashō*, which gave him his name. The hut burned down in 1682, and his mother died the following year.

From 1684 he spent much of his life on the road. The longest walk, in 1689, took him some 2,400 kilometres through northern Honshū with his companion Kawai Sora, and became [*Oku no Hosomichi*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oku_no_Hosomichi). He fell ill in Osaka in 1694 and died there among his disciples, and was buried, as he had asked, at Gichū-ji beside Lake Biwa.

poem.jp: 古池や蛙飛びこむ水の音
poem.en: An old pond: a frog jumps in, the sound of the water
poem.note: Spring 1686, at the Fukagawa hut. That April the poets of Edo held a frog contest in its honour

cats: Bashō left no famous cat of his own; the season word did the work for him. *Neko no koi*, “cats in love”, was a set spring topic, and haikai, unlike courtly verse, was allowed to be earthy about it.

In his hands the cats’ affair turns into a small comedy of household architecture: the tomcat slipping in through a gap in the crumbling stove, the she-cat grown thin on barley rice and love. It is the same eye that found a whole season in a frog jumping into a pond: amused, a little sorry for everyone, one creature at a time.

asides.title: A name that grew in the yard
asides.text: Before he was Bashō he signed himself Sōbō, then Tōsei. The name that stuck came from the banana plant his students set by the door of the Fukagawa hut.

asides.title: Divine, briefly
asides.text: In 1793 the Shinto authorities deified him, and for a while criticising his poems was, quite literally, blasphemy.

asides.title: Shiki’s demolition job
asides.text: A century later Masaoka Shiki made his name partly by attacking the Bashō worship he had inherited, and in the same stroke helped bring Bashō to modern readers.

asides.title: A crater with his name
asides.text: In 1979 the International Astronomical Union named a crater on Mercury after him.

author: Ikenishi Gonsui
name: Ikenishi Gonsui

images.caption: Portrait of Ikenishi Gonsui, by an unknown artist.

lifeText.text: Ikenishi Gonsui was born in Nara into a family of town elders and is said to have taken a priest’s robe at sixteen to give himself to haikai. He made his name in Edo in the salon of the daimyō poet Naitō Fūko, compiled several anthologies and knew Bashō’s circle, then moved to Kyoto in 1682 and travelled widely, as far as Sado and Kyushu. He died in Kyoto in 1722.

cats: His cats belong to night scenes: a cat bolts, and the plum tree shakes under a hazy moon; at the kitchen god’s festival a cat takes the flute part in the sacred dance.

asides.title: Gonsui of the winter wind
asides.text: His poem “the winter wind has an end after all: the sound of the sea” earned him the nickname Kogarashi no Gonsui, and was imitated by Sōseki and Akutagawa.

timeline.text: Moves to Kyoto; travels north and west

headings.timeline: From Nagasaki to the hut of fallen persimmons

lifeText.text: Kyorai was born in Nagasaki, the second son of a Confucian physician, and was sent to Kyoto at eight to train in the martial arts. He served noble households until his mid-twenties, then never took another post.

In 1684 he met Takarai Kikaku and through him entered Bashō’s school; a few years later he met the master in Edo and became one of his most trusted disciples. With Nozawa Bonchō he compiled the anthology *Sarumino* (1691). His cottage at Saga, [Rakushisha](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E8%90%BD%E6%9F%BF%E8%88%8E), was a favourite stop for Bashō. After Bashō’s death Kyorai wrote down what the master had taught, and his *Kyoraishō* is still the richest record of what Bashō actually said. He died in 1704.

poem.jp: 岩鼻やここにもひとり月の客
poem.en: On the rocky point: here, too, is one more guest of the moon
poem.note: Bashō told him to read it as the poet announcing himself to the moon

cats: Kyorai is the disciple who wrote things down, and his own verse has the same patience. What he took from Bashō was *sabi*, the beauty of things left alone and slightly worn.

His cats are small and slightly put-upon: a kitten worrying the strings of a purse on a summer evening, a cat bitten by a fickle friend and left gazing at the sky. Nothing much happens, and the poem lets it not happen: *sabi*, with whiskers.

asides.title: Haikai’s regional magistrate
asides.text: Admired for his integrity, he was nicknamed “the haikai magistrate of the thirty-three western provinces”.

asides.title: The persimmons fell in one night
asides.text: His cottage is called Rakushisha, “the hut of fallen persimmons”, after the night every persimmon on its trees came down at once. Bashō stayed there three times.

asides.title: A family of poets
asides.text: His wife Kana-jo and his sister Chine-jo were haiku poets too.

author: Hattori Ransetsu
name: Hattori Ransetsu

images.file: Three Poets- Mukai Kyorai, Hattori Ransetsu, and Shiba Sonome LACMA AC1998.236.1.jpg
images.caption: Yokoi Kinkoku, Three Poets: Mukai Kyorai, Hattori Ransetsu and Shiba Sonome, late 18th–early 19th century. Los Angeles County Museum of Art.

lifeText.text: Hattori Ransetsu came from a family of minor samurai from Awaji and was probably born in Edo. He served a daimyo for a time, and by every account he was a wild young man, a regular of the theatres and the pleasure quarters.

Around 1674 he became one of Bashō’s earliest students, and by 1688 he was a master in his own right. Bashō called him and Kikaku the peach and the cherry of his garden, and after Bashō’s death the two disciples divided Edo haikai between them. When news of the master’s death reached Edo in 1694, Ransetsu gathered the school for a memorial meeting that same day and set out for the grave at [Gichū-ji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gich%C5%AB-ji). He died in 1707; his line, the Setsumon, long outlived him.

poem.jp: 梅一輪一輪ほどの暖かさ
poem.en: One plum blossom: one blossom’s worth of warmth
poem.note: Early spring, counted out one blossom at a time

cats: Ransetsu’s verse is quiet, and critics from his own day onward found it gentle to a fault. R. H. Blyth heard something else in it: a real sympathy for living things.

His cats bear Blyth out. He burns aloeswood for a cat in love and sends it off; he asks a child to build a snake and an owl as well as a snow cat; he notices a cat feeling the chill while a deer calls under the thirteenth-night moon. Gentle, yes, but always watching something alive.

asides.title: Peach and cherry
asides.text: On the Doll Festival of 1692 Bashō wrote: “In my hut, peach and cherry; among my students, Kikaku and Ransetsu.”

asides.title: Flowers, no fruit?
asides.text: A critic of his own time called him “a man of small calibre… he seems to have flowers, but has no fruit.”

asides.title: Leaves on the wind
asides.text: His death poem: 一葉散る咄ひとはちる風の上, “A leaf falls; ah, another falls, on the wind.”

author: Shiinomoto Saimaro
name: Shiinomoto Saimaro

lifeText.text: Shiinomoto Saimaro was born in Uda in Yamato, adopted into a retainer family and lost his place, it is said, over some misstep. He studied haikai first with Yamamoto Saimu and then with the novelist and poet Ihara Saikaku, taking a character from each teacher’s name in turn. In Edo from 1677 he moved in Bashō’s circle and knew [Takarai Kikaku](#/poet/takarai-kikaku); from 1689 he lived in Osaka for good, where, with the backing of [Uejima Onitsura](#/poet/uejima-onitsura) and Konishi Raizan, he became one of the leading masters. He died on the second day of the New Year, 1738, by the old calendar.

cats: Saimaro’s cats range from the tender to the decorative: a kitten sniffing at a snail; a Chinese cat, the pampered foreign breed, given a May festival ball and a bead blind; and a cat loved so much it borrows a courtesan’s charms.

asides.title: Names on loan
asides.text: His early pen names were built from his teachers’: Sokubu from Saimu, then Saimaru from Saikaku.

timeline.text: Moves to Edo; meets Bashō’s circle

author: Morikawa Kyoriku
name: Morikawa Kyoriku

headings.cats: A dried sardine and a love song

images.caption: Morikawa Kyoriku, portrait by Watanabe Kazan, from the album Azuma Nishiki-e. National Diet Library.

lifeText.text: Morikawa Kyoriku was a samurai of the Hikone domain, a master of the cross-bladed spear, a student of Chinese verse and a painter trained in the Kanō school. He wrote haikai in the Danrin manner as a young man, then found his way to Bashō’s school through Esa Shōhaku, [Takarai Kikaku](#/poet/takarai-kikaku) and [Hattori Ransetsu](#/poet/hattori-ransetsu).

He became Bashō’s pupil in Edo in 1692 and studied with him for less than ten months: Bashō taught him haikai, and he taught Bashō painting. Back in Hikone he led the local poets, compiled anthologies with [Kōno Riyū](#/poet/kono-riyu), taught [Naoe Mokudō](#/poet/naoe-mokudo), and wrote sharp books of criticism, until a long illness from 1707 ended his life in 1715.

cats: Kyoriku’s cats are lively and a little coarse: a tomcat crying for love with a dried sardine still in his mouth, no tobacco needed for the cats of the Yoshiwara, an old cat sharing in the New Year festivities, a cat rubbing itself on a bamboo shoot.

asides.title: Lessons both ways
asides.text: Bashō taught Kyoriku poetry; Kyoriku, a Kanō-trained painter, taught Bashō to paint.

asides.title: A carved Bashō
asides.text: He is said to have cut down a cherry tree Bashō loved and carved it into a statue of the master for Kawai Chigetsu.

timeline.text: Returns to Hikone with Bashō’s parting text

poem.jp: 十團子も小粒になりぬ秋の風
poem.en: Even the ten dumplings have grown smaller: autumn wind
poem.note: The dumplings sold at Utsu Pass on the Tōkaidō, strung ten to a skewer

author: Ochi Etsujin
name: Ochi Etsujin

headings.timeline: A dyer who walked to Sarashina

lifeText.text: Ochi Etsujin was born in Echigo and ran a dyeing business in Nagoya. He met Bashō in 1684 and became the leading figure of Bashō’s school in Owari, one of the Ten Disciples. In 1688 he went with Bashō to see the moon at Sarashina, the journey of *Sarashina Kikō*. His grave in Nagoya is a city historic site.

cats: His envy of the cats in love made it into *Sarumino*: when they are finished with each other, they are simply finished. Another poem finds them faster than the beans thrown to drive out demons.

asides.title: In Sarumino
asides.text: His cat poem “How I envy them” was chosen for Sarumino, the anthology of Bashō’s school published in 1691.

timeline.text: Meets Bashō and joins his school
His cat poem appears in Sarumino

author: Mizuta Masahide
name: Mizuta Masahide

headings.cats: A cat in love, catching its breath
headings.timeline: The patron of Bashō’s last hut

lifeText.text: Mizuta Masahide was born in Zeze on Lake Biwa and seems to have held a fairly senior place in the domain. He studied with Esa Shōhaku, and in 1688 a single poem made Bashō want to meet him: when his storehouse burned down, Masahide wrote that now nothing stood in the way of the moon. Bashō called it the very soul of poetry. Masahide went on to support Bashō with money and was the main backer of the Mumyōan hut at Gichū-ji, where Bashō is buried. He died in 1723.

cats: His cats are small and weather-beaten: a tomcat in love stopping to catch his breath at the rain barrel, and a cat that goes wandering too when the household moves on an autumn evening.

asides.title: The storehouse and the moon
asides.text: “My storehouse has burned: nothing now to block the moon.” Bashō heard the poem, said this was what poetry was for, and asked to meet the man who wrote it.

asides.title: Keep it simple
asides.text: Bashō wrote asking him to keep the new hut plain, since he lived like a cloud anyway; the result was the Mumyōan, the Nameless Hut.

timeline.text: His storehouse poem wins Bashō’s admiration
Helps build the Mumyōan hut for Bashō

poem.jp: 倉焼けてさはるものなき月見かな
poem.en: My storehouse burned down: now nothing blocks the view of the moon
poem.note: His most quoted verse, a cheerful answer to losing everything

author: Takarai Kikaku
name: Takarai Kikaku

headings.timeline: From boy disciple to Edo’s wit

images.caption: Watanabe Kazan, Portrait of Kikaku. National Diet Library, Tokyo.

lifeText.text: Kikaku was born in Edo, the eldest son of a physician to the lords of Zeze, and joined Bashō while still a boy, around 1673. At twenty-two he edited his first anthology, [*Minashiguri*](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E8%99%9A%E6%A0%97), *Shriveled Chestnuts* (1683), with an afterword by Bashō.

He became a master in 1686 and the most fashionable poet in Edo: a drinker, a wit, and a friend of the painter Hanabusa Itchō and the actor Ichikawa Danjūrō II. After Bashō’s death in 1694 he wrote the account of the master’s last days and edited the memorial anthology *Kareobana*. His later manner, quick, showy and colloquial, came to be called the *share* style. He died in 1707.

poem.jp: 鐘ひとつ売れぬ日はなし江戸の春
poem.en: Not a single day without a temple bell sold: springtime in Edo
poem.note: Edo at its richest. In 2007 it opened an international linked-verse sequence marking 300 years since his death

cats: When Kikaku wrote at length about a flea bite, Bashō compared him to Fujiwara no Teika, the court poet famous for making grand verse out of small matters. It was meant as half a compliment.

A poet who could make a flea bite epic is built for cats: Kikaku’s kittens tumble over each other with a butterfly, and a cricket’s widow sings on for the one the cat ate. Small matters, full theatrical lighting.

asides.title: Not Enomoto
asides.text: He is often listed as Enomoto Kikaku. That is a slip: he first used his mother’s family name, Enoshita, and later chose Takarai for himself.

asides.title: The Teika of fleas
asides.text: The flea-bite exchange is preserved in Kyorai’s notes on Bashō’s teaching, the Kyoraishō.

asides.title: A plot he never joined
asides.text: Kabuki has him meeting one of the forty-seven ronin on the eve of their famous raid and trading verses. The scene is a later invention.

author: Uejima Onitsura
name: Uejima Onitsura

headings.cats: Telling the time by a cat’s eyes
headings.timeline: From Itami to a prize in his name

images.caption: Uejima Onitsura, from an 18th-century portrait. Itami City.

lifeText.text: Onitsura was the third son of a prominent sake brewer in [Itami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Itami,_Hy%C5%8Dgo), near Osaka, and was writing haikai as a child. At thirteen he studied with Matsue Shigeyori, and later he joined the Danrin school of Nishiyama Sōin.

At twenty-five he went to Osaka to study medicine, then served several domains as an accountant and steward. Through friends in Bashō’s circle he came to know Bashō himself. In 1718 he published *Hitorigoto*, *Talking to Myself*, with its famous line that outside sincerity there is no haikai, and people began to speak of “Bashō in the east, Onitsura in the west.” He died in Osaka in 1738.

poem.jp: 行水の捨てどころなし虫の声
poem.en: Nowhere to throw out the bathwater: insects singing
poem.note: An autumn evening: wherever he might pour the bath, there are insects singing

cats: Onitsura’s whole programme fits in one word, *makoto*, sincerity: say what is there, without ornament.

His cats are observed the same way. A tomcat in love who cannot sit still even in the sun; a spring day when the cat’s narrowed pupils say it is not yet past noon, the old trick of reading the hour from a cat’s eyes. No ornament, just what is there.

asides.title: Sake first
asides.text: His family were among the leading brewers of Itami, a town famous for sake.

asides.title: East and west
asides.text: “Bashō in the east, Onitsura in the west”: the pairing put an Osaka poet level with the master.

asides.title: An autumn day of his own
asides.text: The poet Kawahigashi Hekigotō made Onitsura-ki, the anniversary of his death, an autumn season word.

timeline.text: Born in Itami to a family of sake brewers

author: Naitō Jōsō
name: Naitō Jōsō

headings.cats: A wild cat under the winter moon
headings.timeline: From Inuyama to a hermit’s hut by Ōtsu

images.caption: Naitō Jōsō, from an Edo-period portrait.

lifeText.text: Jōsō was born in Inuyama in Owari, the eldest son of a samurai serving the Naruse house, and entered service at fourteen with a master who also wrote haikai. In 1688, at twenty-six, he gave up the samurai life; English sources say his health was the reason.

He met Bashō after the master came back from the north and became one of his Ten Disciples, with poems in *Sarumino* (1691). At Bashō’s deathbed in 1694 his was the verse the master singled out. He mourned Bashō for three years and lived as a recluse near Ōtsu until his death in 1704.

poem.jp: うづくまる薬缶の下のさむさ哉
poem.en: Crouching by the kettle of medicine: the cold
poem.note: Written at Bashō’s deathbed in 1694; the master singled it out

cats: Jōsō is the most inward of Bashō’s students, a samurai turned recluse who wrote about weather, solitude and the occasional flea.

His cats keep the same company: a stray dashing out from under the eaves into winter moonlight, a cold night by the brazier that leaves both the cat and the poet’s paper robe singed. The stillness of a recluse, with the odd burn mark.

asides.title: A flea’s way out
asides.text: In Sarumino: 隙明や蚤の出て行耳の穴, “Free at last: a flea makes its way out through my ear.”

asides.title: Three years in mourning
asides.text: When Bashō died, Jōsō mourned him for three full years.

asides.title: One of the Ten
asides.text: He is counted among the Shōmon Jittetsu, Bashō’s ten great disciples.

timeline.text: Writes the kettle poem at Bashō’s deathbed

author: Kōno Riyū
name: Kōno Riyū

headings.timeline: A temple priest in Bashō’s circle

lifeText.text: Kōno Riyū was the fourteenth head priest of Meishō-ji, a Pure Land temple near Hikone, from a family claiming descent from the Kōno warriors of Iyo. In 1691, on the pretext of temple business, he went to see Bashō at [Mukai Kyorai](#/poet/mukai-kyorai)’s cottage in Saga, where Bashō was writing his *Saga Diary*, and became his pupil. With [Morikawa Kyoriku](#/poet/morikawa-kyoriku) he compiled several anthologies in 1702. He died in 1705.

cats: His two cat poems mix the old and the fashionable: cats in love at the crumbling Fuwa barrier house, a ruin famous in classical poetry, and a cat’s paw done up Edo style in summer clothes.

asides.title: The hat mound
asides.text: After Bashō died, Riyū was given his teacher’s worn bamboo hat and buried it in the temple grounds as a memorial mound.

asides.title: Four plums
asides.text: He called himself Shibairo, “the four-plum hut”, after the four plum trees in the temple garden.

timeline.text: Visits Bashō at Rakushisha and joins his school
Compiles Infutagi and Uda no Hōshi with Kyoriku

author: Kagami Shikō
name: Kagami Shikō

headings.timeline: From temple boy to his own funeral

images.caption: Kagami Shikō, portrait by Watanabe Kazan, from the album Azuma Nishiki-e. National Diet Library.

lifeText.text: Kagami Shikō was born in Mino, lost his father young and was placed in a Zen temple, which he left at about nineteen. He met Bashō in Ōmi in 1690, followed him to Edo, and in 1694 travelled with him from Iga to Osaka, where he nursed the dying master and took down his will.

After Bashō’s death he travelled endlessly, collecting his teacher’s last poems and holding memorial gatherings, and built the Mino school, a line of Bashō’s followers that still exists today. A sharp theorist with a reputation for self-interest, he even staged his own death in 1711 and went on publishing under new names. He died in Mino in 1731.

cats: Shikō’s cats in love are the theorist’s jokes: a cat grown bored with a lap of fine silk, and the observation that a tomcat has no wits to turn himself into a handsome young man, as a proper shape-shifting fox would.

asides.title: A rehearsed funeral
asides.text: In 1711 he announced his own death, held the rites, and then carried on as his own “late teacher” under new names.

asides.title: Bashō’s will
asides.text: At Bashō’s deathbed in Osaka in 1694 it was Shikō who wrote out the master’s will.

asides.title: Chiyo’s publicist
asides.text: In 1719 he visited the young [Kaga no Chiyo-ni](#/poet/kaga-no-chiyo-ni) and spread her fame as a born master.

timeline.text: Kuzu no Matsubara, his first book on poetics
With Bashō on his last journey; writes out his will

author: Naoe Mokudō
name: Naoe Mokudō

headings.timeline: A samurai with the best cherry in Hikone

lifeText.text: Naoe Mokudō was a samurai of the Hikone domain, born into the Uematsu family and adopted by the Naoe. He joined Bashō in the master’s last years, around 1692 to 1694, and wrote that he spent thirty years with [Morikawa Kyoriku](#/poet/morikawa-kyoriku) drinking from Bashō’s stream. Kyoriku recorded that Bashō called him “a rare and remarkable talent”. His collection *Mizu no Oto*, *The Sound of Water*, went to the printer a month before he died.

cats: Mokudō wrote more cats in love than most of Bashō’s pupils, and each one is a different joke: a rough tongue offered as a love gift, a reputation fit for a shamisen skin, a she-cat who must be a courtesan reborn, eyes glinting like the jealous Lady Aoi of the Genji tale.

asides.title: A model for later poets
asides.text: Bashō praised his poem about water running through the spring barley as a model of plain description for generations to come; it gave his collection its title.

asides.title: The garden cherry
asides.text: A later commentary says his house had the earliest-blooming cherry in the domain, with a viewing party every spring.

timeline.text: Sends Mizu no Oto to the printer

author: Yokoi Yayū
name: Yokoi Yayū

images.caption: Yokoi Yayū, as reproduced in a 1939 collection of portraits of Japanese writers.

lifeText.text: Yokoi Yayū was the eldest son of a senior retainer of the Owari domain and inherited the post at twenty-six, rising to high office in Nagoya. He was famous for doing everything: haikai, prose, martial arts, the lute ballads of the Heike, nō chanting, painting, Chinese verse and comic poetry. He learned haikai from followers of [Kagami Shikō](#/poet/kagami-shiko).

At fifty-three he retired on grounds of ill health to a hut in Maezu, now central Nagoya, and spent nearly thirty years writing for pleasure. His haikai prose, collected as *Uzura-goromo*, *The Quail’s Robe*, was published only after his death, by the Edo writer Ōta Nanpo, who had come across a single piece and spent years hunting for the rest.

cats: Yayū’s cats are drawn with the same light hand as his prose: the shadow of a cat scratching its ear under plum-scented air, and a cat sleeping off a grudge by the smoke hole, as if its feelings were going up the chimney.

asides.title: The ghost that was pampas grass
asides.text: The proverb “the ghost turned out to be withered pampas grass” is a smoothed-down version of one of his haiku, recorded in an 1816 book of eccentric poets.

asides.title: Found by accident
asides.text: Ōta Nanpo read one of Yayū’s pieces in a temple, copied it out because it was too good to leave, and later published the whole collection.

asides.title: Ten rules for health
asides.text: A set of ten health maxims is attributed to him, among them less meat, more vegetables; less riding, more walking; less anger, more laughter.

timeline.text: Born to a retainer family of the Owari domain
Also made commissioner of temples and shrines
Retires to his hut at Maezu
Ōta Nanpo begins publishing The Quail’s Robe

author: Kaga no Chiyo-ni
name: Kaga no Chiyo-ni

headings.cats: Lost in the snow for love
headings.timeline: From scroll mounter’s daughter to nun

images.image_credit: Ogata GekkôOgata Gekkô died 1920; Takekawa Risaburô

images.caption: Utagawa Kunisada, Kaga no Chiyo, from Famous Women Past and Present, 1859. National Diet Library.

lifeText.text: Chiyo was born in Matto, in Kaga Province, the daughter of a scroll mounter, and was writing haikai as a child. At about seventeen she went to see Kagami Shikō, one of Bashō’s disciples, who was passing through. He asked for a poem on the cuckoo, she kept composing all night until one satisfied him, and her name spread across Japan.

Whether she married is disputed. The traditional story gives her a husband in Kanazawa who died young, but Japanese scholars find no firm evidence for him, or for the wedding poem usually quoted as proof. What is certain is that she went on writing, in Matto, for the rest of her life.

In 1754 she shaved her head and became a nun under the name Soen. Ten years later her domain chose her to prepare its gifts for a Korean embassy: twenty-one works on her own haiku. In her seventies she wrote the preface to an anthology edited by Buson. She died in 1775, leaving some 1,700 poems.

poem.jp: 朝顔に釣瓶とられてもらひ水
poem.en: Morning glory: the well bucket taken by its vine, I go and borrow water
poem.note: She later revised the opening to “Asagao ya”, the version Kanazawa still prefers

cats: Her famous poem is about not disturbing a living thing: rather than tear the vine off the bucket, she walks to the neighbours for water.
Her cats get the same courtesy. One pushes through snowdrifts and loses his way for love; in another poem the parting comes not with a scene but with silence, when the crying simply stops.

asides.title: Not her poem
asides.text: “Waking, sleeping, how wide the mosquito net is” is widely quoted as Chiyo’s, but it was written before her, by a courtesan called Ukihashi.

asides.title: Shiki was not impressed
asides.text: Masaoka Shiki called the morning-glory poem too vulgar to count as haiku. D. T. Suzuki thought it showed how deeply she had been struck by the flower.

asides.title: A town in flower
asides.text: Her home town, now Hakusan, made the morning glory its city flower and holds a morning-glory festival in her name.

timeline.text: Born in Matto, daughter of a scroll mounter
Passes Kagami Shikō’s all-night test and becomes famous
Prepares her domain’s gifts for the Korean embassy
Writes a preface for Buson’s anthology Tamamoshū

author: Tan Taigi
name: Tan Taigi

headings.cats: Yowling on the roof, then silence
headings.timeline: Edo, the north, then the pleasure quarter

lifeText.text: Taigi was born in Edo and learned haikai in the city’s Edo-za circle, with friends in the theatre and the pleasure quarters. After travels in the north he moved to Kyoto in 1751 and visited Kyushu the following year.

From 1754 he lived in Kyoto’s [Shimabara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shimabara,_Kyoto) pleasure quarter under the patronage of the house of Kikyōya. There he kept a hermitage, the Fuyaan, where he enshrined Bashō and taught the courtesans haikai and handwriting. In the 1760s he joined Buson’s poetry circle, and the two led the revival of Bashō’s style. He died in Shimabara in 1771; his *Selected Poems* were published for the first anniversary of his death.

poem.jp: 初恋や燈籠によする顔と顔
poem.en: First love: two faces drawn close at the lantern
poem.note: The lanterns of Bon. In Shimabara he is credited with bringing the lantern custom back

cats: Taigi spent seventeen years in Shimabara teaching courtesans to write, and few poets watched courtship as closely.
The season word for cats in love suited him perfectly: the yowling on the roof, and then the sudden silence of the room.

asides.title: Tan, not Sumi
asides.text: The first character of his name, 炭, means charcoal and can be read “sumi”, but he is Tan Taigi.

asides.title: Lanterns back on
asides.text: He is credited with reviving Shimabara’s autumn custom of hanging lanterns through the quarter.

asides.title: His students, by name
asides.text: The courtesans whose verses appear in his New Year collections can be matched to real women in the quarter’s guidebook.

timeline.text: Moves to Kyoto after travels in the north
Settles in Shimabara and opens the Fuyaan
A last visit to old friends in Edo
Taigi Kusen, his Selected Poems, published

author: Yosa Buson
name: Yosa Buson

headings.cats: A silver cat, a golden butterfly
headings.timeline: Forgotten as a poet, found again by Shiki

images.caption: Portrait of Buson by his student Matsumura Goshun.

images.file: Yosa Buson - Sea in Spring - 2015.79.129 - Minneapolis Institute of Art.jpg
images.caption: Yosa Buson, Sea in Spring. Minneapolis Institute of Art.

images.file: Yosa Buson - Kite and two crows - 2013.31.62 - Minneapolis Institute of Art.jpg
images.caption: Yosa Buson, Kite and Two Crows. Minneapolis Institute of Art.

lifeText.text: Buson was born Taniguchi in Kema, a village outside Osaka, and rarely spoke about his childhood; the usual story makes him the son of the village head and a woman in service there. Around twenty he went to Edo and studied haikai with Hayano Hajin at his school, the [Yahantei](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%A4%9C%E5%8D%8A%E4%BA%AD), the Midnight Pavilion.

After Hajin’s death in 1742 he spent years on the road, partly in Bashō’s footsteps through the north, and first signed himself Buson in 1744. In his early forties he settled in Kyoto, taking the name Yosa from his mother’s home region.

Painting paid the bills, and he became one of the great literati painters of his century. He married at about forty-five and had a daughter, Kuno. In 1770 he took over his teacher’s name and school as Yahantei II. He died in Kyoto in 1784, and a century later Masaoka Shiki championed him as the poet who painted in words.

poem.jp: 春の海終日のたりのたりかな
poem.en: The sea in spring: all day long it rises and falls, rises and falls
poem.note: The doubled “notari notari” is the slow swell of the sea itself

cats: Buson wrote like the painter he was, and Shiki prized exactly that: a Buson poem is a picture you could hang.

His cats come out the same way, as compositions: peonies with a silver cat and a golden butterfly, a cat chewing a moonflower with its mind elsewhere, a cat calling for its mate in an old post town of two or three houses, and no mate coming.

asides.title: A painter by trade
asides.text: In his lifetime his paintings were far better received than his poems, and they, not the poems, were his living.

asides.title: A scroll of monsters
asides.text: Between 1754 and 1757 he painted the Buson Yōkai Emaki, a handscroll of ghosts and goblins.

asides.title: Rescued by Shiki
asides.text: Shiki’s essay The Haiku Poet Buson (1896–97) made the case that Buson was Bashō’s equal.

timeline.text: Goes to Edo and studies with Hayano Hajin
Hajin dies; years of travel begin
First publishes under the name Buson
Begins his scroll of ghosts and goblins
Becomes Yahantei II, heir to his teacher’s school
Shiki’s essay on Buson revives his fame as a poet

author: Tachibana Hokushi
name: Tachibana Hokushi

headings.timeline: The sword polisher who walked with Bashō

lifeText.text: Tachibana Hokushi was born in Komatsu in Kaga and worked as a sword polisher in Kanazawa with his elder brother Bokudō. Both brothers appear in haikai anthologies from 1680 onward, first in the Danrin manner.

When Bashō reached Kanazawa on the journey of *Oku no Hosomichi* in 1689, the brothers became his pupils, and Hokushi walked with him for twenty-five days as far as Matsuoka in Echizen. He wrote down what Bashō taught along the way, and became the senior figure of the Bashō school in the Hokuriku, though without much appetite for running it. He died in Kanazawa in 1718.

cats: His cats are northern and nocturnal: a cat’s ears pricked late into a night of winter wind, and a fish-weir keeper wondering whether the cat-eating kite is really the filthy one.

asides.title: Better than the master’s draft
asides.text: Bashō once showed him a poem ending “autumn mountain”; Hokushi said the word sat too heavily and narrowed the view. Bashō went back to “autumn wind” and praised him for it.

asides.title: Burned out, unbowed
asides.text: When a fire in Kanazawa destroyed his house in 1690 he wrote that it had burned, but the blossoms had finished falling first. Bashō’s circle was delighted.

asides.title: A farewell fan
asides.text: Parting at Matsuoka, Bashō gave him a poem about writing on a fan and tearing it in two.

timeline.text: First appears in print, with his brother Bokudō
Joins Bashō in Kanazawa and walks with him for 25 days
A statue of his parting from Bashō is set up at Tenryū-ji, Matsuoka

author: Miyake Shōzan
name: Miyake Shōzan

lifeText.text: Miyake Shōzan ran a pawnshop in Kyoto and lectured at the Ninna-ji and Shōren-in temples, a scholar who also happened to be a senior haikai master. He edited classical texts, translated Chinese vernacular novels, and in 1763 argued in *Haikai Kosen* for a return to the poetry of Bashō’s generation, which made his name. He wrote linked verse with [Tan Taigi](#/poet/tan-taigi) and knew Buson. He was remembered as upright and of few words, and died in 1801 at eighty-four.

cats: Shōzan’s two cat poems are the work of a reserved man irritated by noise: cats in love chasing over the roofs as if across the river of the Dōjōji legend, and a plain complaint that what he cannot stand is how little they care.

asides.title: Novels from China
asides.text: Besides haikai he published Japanese versions of Chinese vernacular fiction, including a life of the mad monk Jigong.

timeline.text: Haikai Kosen calls for a return to Bashō’s era
Writes twenty linked-verse sequences with Taigi

author: Kaya Shirao
name: Kaya Shirao

lifeText.text: Kaya Shirao was born in Fukagawa, the second son of a samurai of the Ueda domain posted to Edo. He studied haikai with Shirai Chōsui’s school, and in 1769 raised a stone with one of Bashō’s poems at the temple of Mount Obasute.

Expelled from his school in 1775, he took his own pupils on the road, then in 1780 opened his Shunjūan studio in Edo and built a large following in the Kantō; his pupils were said to number four thousand. Counted with Buson among the revivers of Bashō’s style, he never married, lived simply, and wrote plain, tender poems. He died in 1791.

cats: Shirao’s cats in love are written with his usual unfussy feeling: a she-cat whose mate has grown distant, a tomcat let out of the door into the night, and cats still at it on the sixth night of the year, when the old year turns.

asides.title: A Japanese Li Bai
asides.text: His poverty and his refusal to marry earned him the nickname “the Li Bai of Japan”.

timeline.text: Born in Fukagawa, Edo, on 3 October
Raises a Bashō stone at Obasute
Expelled from his school; takes to the road

author: Matsuoka Seira
name: Matsuoka Seira

lifeText.text: Matsuoka Seira was born in Edo to a Himeji domain samurai and grew up there, but was sent home for bad conduct and then banished from the domain at twenty-three, gambling being the usual suspicion. He wandered as a poet, settled in Kakogawa in Harima in 1767, took the tonsure on the anniversary of Bashō’s death, and built a large following among the region’s village headmen. He raised memorials to Bashō at Akashi and on Awaji, and died in Kakogawa in 1791.

cats: His cats in love are a gambler’s cats: a tom who will cry until he grows horns, and a stray whose road to love has a trap waiting on it.

asides.title: The greatest symbolist
asides.text: The novelist Nakamura Shin’ichirō wrote that he discovered Seira one New Year as a student and thought him the greatest symbolist among Edo poets.

asides.title: The octopus pot mound
asides.text: At Akashi he raised a stone with Bashō’s poem about octopus pots and brief dreams under the summer moon.

timeline.text: Takes the tonsure on Bashō’s death day
Honoured as a haikai master by the Nijō family

author: Takai Kitō
name: Takai Kitō

lifeText.text: Takai Kitō was the second son of the Kyoto haikai master Takai Kikei, grew up among poets and took the first character of his father’s name as his own.

At thirty he became a pupil of [Yosa Buson](#/poet/yosa-buson), who seems to have meant him as his successor. The two travelled together through Osaka and the Inland Sea coast in 1779; after Buson’s death Kitō compiled the memorial anthology and *Buson Kushū*, the standard collection of his teacher’s poems, and took the title Yahantei III. The great Kyoto fire of 1788 left him moving between pupils’ houses, and he died the following year at forty-nine.

cats: Kitō’s cats are household comedy with good timing: one snug in the fork of a plum tree, one tied up by the leg with a koto string and still in love, and a house so fond of blowfish that even the cat gets blowfish soup.

asides.title: He made Buson’s book
asides.text: Buson Kushū, the collection most readers know Buson’s haiku from, was edited by Kitō after his teacher’s death.

asides.title: Three generations of Midnight
asides.text: The school name Yahantei, Midnight Pavilion, passed from Hayano Hajin to Buson and then to Kitō.

timeline.text: Born in Kyoto, son of the poet Takai Kikei
Travels with Buson to Osaka and the Inland Sea
Edits Buson’s memorial collection and Buson Kushū

author: Narita Sōkyū
name: Narita Sōkyū

lifeText.text: Narita Sōkyū was the son of a Kanazawa samurai. He studied with Takakuwa Rankō, and when his father died in prison and the family stipend was confiscated, he went to Kyoto and relied on his teacher, later inheriting Rankō’s Bashō Hall in the eastern hills. From 1835 he lived in a hut near Yasaka and led the haikai world of the Tenpō era, one of its three great masters with Sakurai Baishitsu and Tagawa Hōrō. He died in 1842.

cats: His cats in love arrive too early and hide badly: barely two days after the New Year pines go up, through the thin reeds where the neighbour’s house shows, peering out from behind the wild asters.

asides.title: A family disgrace
asides.text: His father’s death in prison and the loss of the family’s stipend sent him from Kanazawa to Kyoto.

timeline.text: Takes over Rankō’s Bashō Hall in Kyoto
Moves to a hut near Yasaka

author: Kobayashi Issa
name: Kobayashi Issa

images.caption: Portrait of Issa by Muramatsu Shunpo. Issa Memorial Hall, Shinano.
Oraga Haru, first edition, 1852. Nagano Prefectural Library.
Oraga Haru, 1852: the page with the poem that gave the book its title. Nagano Prefectural Library.

lifeText.text: Issa was born Kobayashi Yatarō in Kashiwabara, a post town in the snowy uplands of [Shinano Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinano_Province). His mother died when he was three and his doting grandmother when he was fourteen. A year later his father sent him to [Edo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edo), largely to end the boy’s feud with his stepmother.

The next ten years leave almost no trace. When Issa reappears he is a working haikai poet, loosely attached to the Nirokuan school, under a pen name meaning “one cup of tea”. He spent the 1790s walking through western Japan, the 1800s in a lawsuit with his half-brother over their father’s land, and came home at forty-nine with half of it.

Marriage to Kiku followed, then the deaths of all four of their children and of Kiku herself. He wrote through every one of them, more than twenty thousand haiku in all, about ten times the number of verses left by [Bashō](#/poet/matsuo-basho). His account of the year his daughter died, *Oraga Haru*, is still the book most readers meet him through.

poem.jp: 露の世は露の世ながらさりながら
poem.en: The world of dew is the world of dew, and yet, and yet
poem.note: Written after the death of his daughter Sato, 1819

cats: Issa’s cats are strays, thieves and lovers: rarely pets, never ornaments. He belonged to [Jōdo Shinshū](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C5%8Dd%C5%8D_Shinsh%C5%AB), the Pure Land school that promises rebirth to anyone who trusts Amida’s vow, and he wrote small creatures as fellow passengers: nearly two hundred poems on frogs, some two hundred and thirty on fireflies and more than a hundred on fleas. Cats get the same courtesy.

The spring season word 猫の恋 *neko no koi*, “cats in love”, lets him write the yowling on the roof with open sympathy. Indoors, the house cat is scolded, fed and forgiven, a quiet stand-in for the family he kept losing. Almost half the poems in this dossier are his, more than any other poet’s.

asides.title: Behind the pen name
asides.text: Registered at birth as Kobayashi Nobuyuki and called Yatarō as a child. 一茶 Issa, “one cup of tea”, is a pen name.

asides.title: Frogs, fleas, fireflies
asides.text: Some 200 poems on frogs, 230 on fireflies, 150 on mosquitoes, 90 on flies and over 100 on fleas: about a thousand verses on small creatures.

asides.title: A death in two calendars
asides.text: He died in the eleventh month of the old lunar year, which fell on 5 January 1828. That is why many sources still give 1827.

asides.title: Last address: a storehouse
asides.text: After the fire of 1827 he lived in his windowless clay storehouse. “The fleas have fled the burning house and taken refuge with me here.” It is now a National Historic Site.

asides.title: A snail in Salinger
asides.text: His snail climbing Mount Fuji turns up in Salinger’s *Franny and Zooey* (1961) and gave the Strugatsky brothers the title of *The Snail on the Slope*.

Father dies; Last Days of My Father

link.label: A son’s notes from the sickbed

timeline.text: Begins the Shichiban Nikki, his “Number Seven Journal”
Comes home to Kashiwabara at forty-nine
First son, Sentarō, lives less than a month
Daughter Sato dies; writes Oraga Haru
Kiku dies. “Outliving them, / outliving them all, / ah, the cold!”

Daughter Yata born after his death

author: Tsuruta Takuchi
name: Tsuruta Takuchi

lifeText.text: Tsuruta Takuchi was born into a family of indigo dyers in Okazaki, in Mikawa. At seventeen he became a pupil of Katō Kyōtai of Owari and also studied with Inoue Shirō, and he grew into the central figure of haikai in the Mikawa region, counted with Sakurai Baishitsu, [Narita Sōkyū](#/poet/narita-sokyu) and Tagawa Hōrō among the “four old men of Tenpō”. He was known as good-natured and fond of drink. He died in Okazaki in 1846, aged seventy-six.

cats: Takuchi’s cats are working animals of a river town: during the early summer rains a boatman comes to borrow a cat, presumably for the rats aboard, and on a stormy night a tomcat in love pricks up his ears.

asides.title: His papers in the library
asides.text: In 1987 his family papers, scrolls and travel diaries went to Okazaki city, which keeps them as the Tsuruta Takuchi collection; several are listed cultural properties.

timeline.text: Born in Okazaki, Mikawa, to a dyer’s family
Becomes a pupil of Katō Kyōtai
His papers are given to the city of Okazaki

author: Inoue Seigetsu
name: Inoue Seigetsu

headings.timeline: Thirty years on the road in Ina

images.caption: Inoue Seigetsu, by Hashizume Gyokusai, an Ina valley painter he worked with.

lifeText.text: Almost nothing certain is known about Inoue Seigetsu’s early life. He told a domain elder that his real name was Inoue Katsuzō and that he came from the Nagaoka domain in Echigo, and some vowel slips in his poems sound like Echigo dialect, but the records that could prove it are lost.

Around 1858, in his late thirties, he simply appeared in the Ina valley of Shinano and wandered there for the next thirty years. A fine calligrapher and a capable teacher, he was fed, lodged and plied with drink by the valley’s amateur poets in return for lessons and inscriptions, while the women and children who saw him lice-ridden and drunk called him “Beggar Seigetsu”. He died there in 1887. Akutagawa and [Santōka](#/poet/taneda-santoka) later admired him.

cats: His cats belong to a man with no house of his own. Even his precious cat is out on a hazy spring night; the shadow of a cat said to be in love falls across a paper screen; and the cats in love seem to be chased along by the lengthening days.

asides.title: Beggar Seigetsu
asides.text: Wealthy amateurs treated him as a master; the valley’s children called him a beggar. Both, by the accounts, were right.

asides.title: A name on a letter
asides.text: One of the few traces of his real name is a single letter to a sake brewer who looked after him, signed Inoue Katsuzō.

timeline.text: Probably born, perhaps in Nagaoka, Echigo
A haiku of his appears in a memorial collection printed in Nagano
Asks a Takatō domain elder to preface his anthology Echigo Jishi
Dies in the Ina valley on 10 March

author: Naitō Meisetsu
name: Naitō Meisetsu

headings.timeline: A samurai who took a pupil for a teacher

images.caption: Naitō Meisetsu, photograph.

lifeText.text: Naitō Meisetsu was born in the Edo residence of the Matsuyama domain to a senior samurai family, fought in the second expedition against Chōshū as a young page, and after the Restoration worked in education, rising to a post in the Ministry of Education. In 1887 he became warden of a hostel for young men from Matsuyama in Tokyo, where his charges included [Masaoka Shiki](#/poet/masaoka-shiki) and Kawahigashi Hekigotō.

In 1892 he made Shiki, twenty-one years his junior, his haiku teacher, and became the grand old man of Shiki’s circle, judging newspaper haiku columns and lecturing on Buson’s poems in *Hototogisu*. He died in 1926.

cats: His cats are drawn with an old man’s amused affection: a kitten grabbing at a ball that knows nothing of love yet, a tomcat’s love as one-sided as an abalone’s single shell, and the grasses of love growing on a cat’s grave in the light rain.

asides.title: Whatever happens
asides.text: His pen name Meisetsu is a pun on a phrase meaning “leave everything to how things turn out”.

asides.title: A boyhood playmate
asides.text: As a child he played with a young servant at the domain residence, Harada Sanosuke, later a captain of the Shinsengumi.

timeline.text: Becomes warden of the Tokiwa hostel
Takes Shiki as his haiku teacher

author: Murakami Kijō
name: Murakami Kijō

images.caption: Murakami Kijō on Kannonyama, Takasaki, in 1937.

lifeText.text: Murakami Kijō was born in Edo, the son of a Tottori samurai, moved to Takasaki as a boy and was adopted into his mother’s family. Deafness ended his hopes of a military career, and he spent his whole working life in Takasaki as a court scrivener, raising ten children in steady poverty. He wrote to Masaoka Shiki for advice, sent poems to *Hototogisu* for years, and from 1913 was one of its central poets under Kyoshi. He died in 1938.

cats: Kijō is the poet of the hard-up and the overlooked, and his cats fit: a cat abandoned in the bindweed and crying, a black cat lapping water from the rice seedbed, a temple cat fighting a snake in barley harvest, a kitten that sets a toad’s heart pounding, a cat that comes home in a thunderstorm.

asides.title: The poet of the mind’s ear
asides.text: His motto was “the mind’s ear”, after the familiar “mind’s eye”, and he is remembered by that phrase.

asides.title: Fired and rehired
asides.text: Dismissed from his scrivener’s post at fifty-one, he got it back with the help of a lawyer from Kyoshi’s circle.

author: Masaoka Shiki
name: Masaoka Shiki

images.caption: Masaoka Shiki, Self-portrait, 1900. National Diet Library.
Shiki photographed around 1890. National Diet Library.
Shiki in baseball uniform, 1889.
Masaoka Shiki, Fruit, painted from his sickbed in 1902.
A commemorative photograph taken in Shinbashi, Tokyo, November 1883. Shiki is at the right of the front row.

lifeText.text: Shiki was born Masaoka Tsunenori in Matsuyama, into a samurai family of modest means. His father died when he was a small boy, and his grandfather, the Confucian scholar Ōhara Kanzan, started him on the Chinese classics. At fifteen he caught the political fever of the Freedom and People’s Rights Movement, and in 1883 he left school for Tokyo.

In Tokyo he found baseball and haiku, and a friend in a classmate called Natsume Kinnosuke, the future [Sōseki](#/poet/natsume-soseki). In 1889 he coughed blood for the first time and took the name Shiki, after the cuckoo said to sing until it spits blood. He left the Imperial University, joined the newspaper *Nippon* in 1892 and began his campaign to reform haiku. In 1895 he went to China as a war correspondent, arrived after the fighting had stopped, and came home seriously ill.

He convalesced in Matsuyama at Sōseki’s lodgings, then went back to Tokyo, where from about 1897 he was mostly confined to bed in Negishi. Disciples gathered round him, and the magazine [*Hototogisu*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hototogisu_(magazine)) spread his ideas. He wrote to the end: his sickbed column *A Six-Foot Sickbed* ran in the paper until two days before he died, in September 1902, at thirty-four.

poem.jp: 柿くへば鐘が鳴るなり法隆寺
poem.en: I bite into a persimmon, and the bell rings out at Hōryū-ji
poem.note: Nara, autumn 1895, on a trip Sōseki helped pay for: a reply to Sōseki’s own bell poem

cats: Shiki’s great idea was *shasei*, sketching from life: no puns, no borrowed sentiment, just what is in front of you.

Many of his cat poems come from *Kanzan Rakuboku*, the notebooks of his apprentice years: dozens of variations on cats in love, worked through like scales. A tomcat crossing the drying pole like a log bridge, two cats glaring from either side of a fence, an earthquake that rolls a lover off the roof. Later, the sketches turn colder: a cat’s cry like a baby’s on a frosty night, a ruined temple with torn banana leaves and not even a cat.

asides.title: A bird that coughs blood
asides.text: 子規, Shiki, is another name for the hototogisu, the little cuckoo said to sing until it coughs blood. He took it the year his tuberculosis showed.

asides.title: Catcher, then poet
asides.text: He played catcher, used the pen name 野球 “No-bōru”, a pun on his own name, Noboru, and was voted into Japan’s Baseball Hall of Fame in 2002.

asides.title: Who paid for the eel
asides.text: In Matsuyama he treated Sōseki to eel on rice, then left Sōseki to pay the bill.

asides.title: Fifty-four pen names
asides.text: In one essay he listed fifty-four pen names he had used, and scholars have found more.

author: Natsume Sōseki
name: Natsume Sōseki

headings.timeline: Matsuyama, London, Tokyo and a 1,000-yen note

images.caption: Natsume Sōseki photographed by Ogawa Kazumasa, September 1912.
Sōseki in October 1912. National Diet Library.
A page of the manuscript of I Am a Cat. National Diet Library.

lifeText.text: Sōseki was born Natsume Kinnosuke in Edo, the unplanned youngest of eight, and was given away twice: first to a couple who dealt in second-hand goods, then to the Shiobara family, who raised him as their own until he was nine. A maid whispered the truth about his parents to him one night, and he was formally restored to the Natsume family only in 1888.

At school he became friends with [Masaoka Shiki](#/poet/masaoka-shiki), his lifelong companion in verse. After the Imperial University he taught English in Matsuyama, the town of [*Botchan*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botchan), and in Kumamoto, married Nakane Kyōko in 1896, and in 1900 was sent to London, where two lonely years ended in a breakdown.

Back in Tokyo, at Takahama Kyoshi’s suggestion, he wrote a comic story narrated by a cat. *I Am a Cat* ran in *Hototogisu* from 1905 and made him famous. In 1907 he left the university to write novels for the *Asahi Shimbun*, among them *Sanshirō*, *And Then* and *Kokoro*. He died in 1916 with *Light and Dark* unfinished, the next instalment number, 189, written on an otherwise blank page.

poem.jp: 此の下に稲妻起る宵あらん
poem.en: Under this, on some evening, lightning will flash
poem.note: Written on the grave marker of his nameless cat, September 1908

cats: The cat came first. In 1904 a small stray got into the house in Sendagi and refused to leave, and the family let it stay without ever giving it a name. A year later it was the narrator of [*I Am a Cat*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Am_a_Cat), the cat who has “as yet no name”.

When it died in September 1908, Sōseki sent his friends a formal death notice, buried it in the garden and wrote a haiku on its grave marker. The next year a short piece called “The Cat’s Grave” appeared among his *Spring Miscellany*.

asides.title: As yet no name
asides.text: The novel opens “I am a cat. As yet I have no name.” The real cat never got one either.

asides.title: On the thousand-yen note
asides.text: His portrait was on the 1,000-yen banknote from 1984 to 2004.

asides.title: Kept for science
asides.text: His brain and stomach were donated to the medical school of Tokyo Imperial University.

asides.title: A novel a year
asides.text: From 1907 until his death he published roughly a novel a year, serialised in the Asahi.

author: Matsuse Seisei
name: Matsuse Seisei

lifeText.text: Matsuse Seisei was born in Osaka, the son of a charcoal merchant, and worked at a bank while he wrote haiku. In 1898 Masaoka Shiki wrote that “in Osaka there is Seisei”. He worked briefly on *Hototogisu* in Tokyo, then went back to Osaka, joined the *Asahi* newspaper, and in 1901 founded his own magazine, which became *Kenchō*, making him the leading haiku master of the Kansai, independent of Kyoshi. He died in 1937.

cats: His two cat poems are spring miniatures: a kitten licking a violet, and a tomcat in love hit with a thread spool.

asides.title: The first modern collection
asides.text: His Tsumaki of 1904 is counted as the earliest personal haiku collection published in its author’s lifetime in the modern era.

timeline.text: Praised by Shiki; joins Hototogisu in Tokyo

author: Terada Torahiko
name: Terada Torahiko

images.caption: Terada Torahiko in 1935, the year of his death.

lifeText.text: Terada Torahiko was born in Tokyo and grew up in Kōchi, a sickly boy given a microscope by his father. At the Fifth Higher School in Kumamoto he met two teachers who shaped his life, the physicist Tamaru Takurō and the English teacher [Natsume Sōseki](#/poet/natsume-soseki), and with Sōseki he founded a haiku circle in 1898. His first wife died young in 1902.

He became one of Japan’s best-known physicists, working on subjects from the acoustics of the shakuhachi to earthquakes and the shapes of cracks, and at the same time a much-loved essayist under the name Yoshimura Fuyuhiko. He died on the last day of 1935.

cats: Torahiko’s cats sit in a scientist’s winter: whiskers coming close to his face on a freezing night, a cat that will not answer however he talks to it, and a grave nobody can name among cat grass, foxtail and grass with no name at all.

asides.title: A doctorate in bamboo flute
asides.text: His doctorate, in 1908, was an acoustic study of the shakuhachi.

asides.title: Taught by Sōseki
asides.text: He met Sōseki as his English teacher in Kumamoto and called him his teacher for life.

author: Taneda Santōka
name: Taneda Santōka

images.caption: Taneda Santōka, photograph, date unknown.

lifeText.text: Taneda Santōka was born Taneda Shōichi, eldest son of a landowning family near Hōfu in Yamaguchi. When he was ten his mother, worn down by his father’s philandering, threw herself into the family well. The family fortune went, a sake brewery he ran failed, and drink did the rest. He became a follower of Ogiwara Seisensui’s free-verse haiku magazine *Sōun*.

In 1925 he was ordained as a Zen monk in Kumamoto and spent most of his remaining years walking western Japan as a mendicant, begging for rice, drinking whatever it bought and writing more than twelve thousand verses. He burned his diaries from before 1930; the ones that survive are full of inns, rain and animals. He died in Matsuyama in 1940.

cats: Santōka’s diaries are full of cats met on the road, almost all of them strays: a hungry cat crying when he has nothing to give, kittens dumped by the roadside, a white one and a black one, a cat that rubs against him at dusk and doesn’t want him to leave. At the pilgrims’ inns the cat cries when the cow does, and a tired traveller finds the cat has got into the foot warmer first.

asides.title: The name
asides.text: Santōka, “fire on the mountain top”, is one of the thirty divination names of the sexagenary cycle. It was not his own birth year’s; he wrote that he simply liked the look and meaning of it.

asides.title: Up in smoke
asides.text: He burned his diaries from before 1930. The later ones, published after his death, are where most of these cat poems come from.

asides.title: A wasted life, he said
asides.text: Late in life he wrote that his had been a life of waste upon waste, with drink poured into it constantly, and the poems born from that.

author: Hasegawa Reiyoshi
name: Hasegawa Reiyoshi

images.caption: Hasegawa Reiyoshi, photograph.

lifeText.text: Hasegawa Reiyoshi was born Tomita Kaizō in Gunma, the son of a policeman. He went to Tokyo as a shop boy and typesetter, sent haiku to newspapers, and caught the eye of Kawahigashi Hekigotō. He married the poet Hasegawa Kanajo in 1909 and took her family name, qualified as a pharmacist, and worked on the editing of *Hototogisu* at Takahama Kyoshi’s request. In 1921 he founded his own magazine, *Kareno*. He died of typhoid at forty-two.

cats: Reiyoshi’s cats are watched without sentiment: a sick cat, not dead yet, staring at him in the autumn wind; kittens dying one by one in a basket; a kitten whose mother has gone; then, more kindly, a cat asleep on the tatami by young bamboo and someone feeding the neighbourhood cats on an autumn night.

asides.title: Two poets, one name
asides.text: He took the surname of his wife, the haiku poet Hasegawa Kanajo, when they married.

author: Akutagawa Ryūnosuke
name: Akutagawa Ryūnosuke

headings.cats: A puddle drunk by a cat

lifeText.text: Akutagawa Ryūnosuke was born in Tokyo and raised by his mother’s family, the Akutagawas. While still a student of English literature at Tokyo Imperial University he published “Rashōmon” (1915) and “The Nose” (1916), which [Natsume Sōseki](#/poet/natsume-soseki) praised, and he became the leading short-story writer of his generation. He also wrote haiku under the name Gaki, “hungry ghost”. He took his own life in 1927, at thirty-five.

cats: His cat haiku are quick and sly: heat shimmer over a puddle being drunk by a cat; the fire in a courting tomcat’s heart as he crosses the puddles; and a wish to offer New Year rice-cake blossoms to a cat from the Imado kilns.

asides.title: Hungry ghost
asides.text: His haiku name, Gaki, means a hungry ghost of Buddhist hell.

asides.title: A prize in his name
asides.text: Japan’s best-known literary award for new writers, the Akutagawa Prize, was founded in his memory in 1935.

poem.jp: 水洟や鼻の先だけ暮れのこる
poem.en: A runny nose: only the tip of my nose still catches the last light of day
poem.note: A winter dusk, and a joke at his own expense

author: Tomita Moppo
name: Tomita Moppo

lifeText.text: Tomita Moppo was born in Mukōjima, Tokyo, into a once-prosperous family reduced to running a small eel shop. A fever in his first year left both his legs paralysed. He never went to school; he learned to read from picture cards and from Iwaya Sazanami’s children’s magazine, and took the name Moppo, “wooden steps”, from the wooden legs he made himself in the hope of walking. Disabled, poor, tubercular and unschooled, he was hailed as the Takuboku of Taishō haiku. He died at twenty-six in the fires after the Great Kantō Earthquake.

cats: Moppo saw the world from the floor of a small house, and his cats are close up: a cat retching on the grass it has eaten, a cat near its time who wants people near, his own cat doing its business among the millet flowers, a stray sniffing at a stone, another peering through a hole in the paper screen.

asides.title: Wooden steps
asides.text: His pen name means “wooden walking”, after the wooden legs he built for himself.

asides.title: Taught by Sazanami
asides.text: He first learned what haiku were from the poems of Iwaya Sazanami, the children’s writer whose magazine taught him to read.

timeline.text: Born in Mukōjima, Tokyo, on 14 April
Dies in the Great Kantō Earthquake, 1 September

author: Kawabata Bōsha
name: Kawabata Bōsha

headings.cats: Cats and butterflies on the hazy road

images.caption: Kawabata Bōsha in the garden of his house, around 1937–38.

lifeText.text: Kawabata Bōsha was born in Tokyo and raised with his half-brother, the painter Kawabata Ryūshi. He trained as a painter himself under Kishida Ryūsei and had a still life accepted for exhibition, but spinal tuberculosis and lung disease ended that path. He turned fully to haiku, became one of Takahama Kyoshi’s favourite pupils in *Hototogisu*, and wrote with a painter’s exactness until his death at forty-three.

cats: His cats in love are painted in soft light: cats and butterflies travelling the same hazy spring road, and a tomcat crooning at the moon.

asides.title: A brother who named his grave
asides.text: His Buddhist death name was chosen by his half-brother Ryūshi.

timeline.text: Becomes a member of the Hototogisu group
